constitutive_assumptions: Friction force acts collinear and opposite to the instantaneous sliding velocity vector via the signum function.
Coulomb friction element represents a quasi-static friction coefficient that is independent of displacement and velocity.
Decoupling assumption: effects of sliding velocity, normal pressure, and frictional heating on the friction coefficient can be treated as separable additive and multiplicative factors.
Normal pressure effect on the coefficient of friction is assumed to be independent of sliding velocity.
All heat generated by frictional dissipation at the contact interface is assumed to flow directly into the steel body.
The steel body is assumed to act as a semi-infinite medium occupying the entire half-space beneath the contact interface with one-dimensional heat conduction normal to the surface.
Thermal radiation at the sliding interface is assumed to be negligible.
The true contact area is assumed to equal the apparent contact area.
The stick-slip (breakaway) force increment decays exponentially as a function of sliding displacement measured from the last motion reversal.
Stick-slip transitions occur only upon sliding direction reversal and do not re-initiate after nonreversing stops in the tested steel-polymer interfaces.
control_variables: Reference initial ambient temperature (T0, approximately 20 degrees Celsius)
Thermal diffusivity (D) and thermal conductivity (k) of steel
Contact surface area of polymer slider (A)
Harmonic sliding motion amplitude and cyclic frequency in testing protocols
dependent_variables: Interface temperature at monitoring points (Ti(t)) and contact-averaged temperature (T(t))

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A three-element parallel friction formulation combining Coulomb friction, a logarithmic velocity-dependent element, and an exponential displacement-dependent stick-slip element accurately models frictional response and static-to-kinetic transitions during cyclic sliding.

Experimental observations demonstrate that the stick-slip effect in steel-polymer interfaces is displacement-dependent rather than purely velocity-dependent, decaying exponentially with displacement from the point of sliding direction reversal.

Specialized cyclic testing protocols with nonreversing intermediate stops show that stick-slip breakaway peaks occur exclusively upon motion direction reversal and are absent when sliding resumes in the same direction.

Frictional heating causes exponential degradation of the coefficient of friction with increasing average contact interface temperature, exhibiting the greatest temperature rise and friction drop near zero displacement in cyclic motion.

In cyclic testing of oil-filled UHMWPE sliding on steel, the proposed displacement-dependent model significantly outperformed existing velocity-dependent and Coulomb models, achieving an R^2 of 0.95 and maximum absolute error of 0.010 compared to R^2 values between 0.00 and 0.74 for previous formulations.

Normal pressure dependence of the friction coefficient can be represented by a hyperbolic tangent modification factor that captures high-pressure reduction while maintaining a finite non-infinite limit as pressure approaches zero.

experimental_setup: Tribology testing apparatus at the John A. Blume Earthquake Engineering Center at Stanford University engineered such that displacements are not directly imposed on a sliding surface, allowing clear separation and identification of stick and reslip instants.

Steel-polymer sliding interfaces consisting of galvanized steel plates in contact with polymer sliders, including oil-filled ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), PTFE, and other polyethylenes/thermoplastics.

Cyclic unidirectional displacement loading protocols including continuous harmonic sliding, protocols with one nonreversing stop per half cycle, and protocols with two nonreversing stops per half cycle.
future_work: Conducting bidirectional sliding experiments to investigate stick-slip behavior under multi-axial displacement paths.
Extending and reformulating the proposed unidirectional friction model into a bidirectional sliding formulation.
Evaluating the influence of bearing stick-slip behavior on the dynamic response of structural secondary systems and building contents during earthquakes.
independent_variables: Displacement at the most recent motion reversal (uR)
Polymer slider material type (oil-filled UHMWPE, PTFE, polyethylenes, various thermoplastics)
Kinematic loading protocol (harmonic cycles, reversing stops, nonreversing stops)
limitations_inferred: Decoupling normal pressure effects from velocity dependence through a single independent multiplicative factor may lose precision for interfaces where pressure sensitivity is strongly velocity-coupled.
Tracking direction reversal states (uR and sign changes) introduces history-dependent state tracking that could present numerical sensitivity during complex multi-frequency or micro-slip vibrations.
Validation is restricted to component-level tribological sliding tests and was not evaluated in coupled structural dynamic shake-table experiments.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The formulation is limited to unidirectional sliding, whereas real seismic isolation bearings slide bidirectionally during earthquake excitations.
Heat conduction assumptions (semi-infinite medium, heat flow exclusively into steel, absence of radiation, true contact area equal to apparent area) do not exactly represent real physical conditions.
Direct measurement of interface temperature during tests is very difficult and interface temperature is non-uniform, requiring the use of computed contact-averaged temperatures.
Model calibration and validation excluded transitional movements to and from rest at the beginning and end of loading protocols, using only fully reversed steady cycles.
While the reversal-only stick-slip rule held for the tested thermoplastics, untested materials might exhibit stick-slip increments after nonreversing stops.
main_results: The proposed five-parameter model achieved an R^2 of 0.95 and a maximum absolute error of 0.010 when fitted to oil-filled UHMWPE experimental cyclic test data, outperforming the Coulomb model (R^2 = 0.00) and four prior models by Lomiento et al. (R^2 = 0.40), Quaglini et al. (R^2 = 0.74), Kumar et al. (R^2 = 0.49), and Gandelli et al. (R^2 = 0.41).
The exponential displacement-dependent element accurately captured the localized breakaway force peak and subsequent decay at motion reversals across different thermoplastics.
The model accurately reproduced hysteretic responses under protocols with nonreversing intermediate stops by updating the reversal displacement uR only when sliding velocity changes sign.

The modular framework successfully accounts for combined effects of velocity, displacement, normal pressure, and frictional heating degradation with fewer or equal parameters compared to existing models.
modeling_methods: Three-element parallel base friction model: Coulomb element (constant quasi-static friction), logarithmic velocity-dependent element, and exponential displacement-dependent stick-slip element.
State-dependent displacement tracking mechanism updating reference displacement uR only upon reversal of the sliding velocity direction.
Thermal degradation modeling using an exponentially decaying temperature factor based on a contact-averaged temperature field.
One-dimensional transient heat conduction formulation solved efficiently using discrete Fourier transforms (DFT / inverse DFT via FFT algorithms).
Pressure modification factor utilizing a hyperbolic tangent functional form to model friction reduction under increasing normal pressure.
Parameter calibration performed through least-squares error minimization against experimental force-displacement hysteretic loops.
performance_metrics: Coefficient of determination (R^2) of the coefficient of friction.
Maximum absolute error (MaxAbsErr) of the coefficient of friction.
Visual goodness-of-fit to experimental normalized force-displacement and force-velocity hysteretic loops.
possible_gap_implications: The displacement-dependent exponential stick-slip formulation and frictional heating decay modeling could provide useful mechanical modeling principles for friction-based sliding joints, cable conduits, and polymer interfaces in mechanical systems and soft robotics, though extension to bidirectional sliding and soft hyperelastic substrates would be required.
paper.research_objective: To develop, calibrate, and validate a modular friction model for steel-polymer sliding interfaces that accounts for variations in sliding velocity, normal pressure, frictional heating degradation, and displacement-dependent stick-slip transitions occurring at motion reversals.
paper.research_problem: The coefficient of friction in steel-polymer sliding interfaces varies instantaneously due to interacting factors (velocity, pressure, frictional heating, and stick-slip transitions); existing models fail to accurately capture the stick-slip breakaway transition that occurs during motion direction reversals.
paper.title: A novel friction model for steel-polymer interfaces in sliding seismic isolation bearings
